articles.title: Driver whose truck drove into Kansas soccer game released, pending toxicology tests
articles.summary: Clipped From Video What began as a soccer game on a sunny Saturday in Wichita, Kansas, for children whose loved ones watched on the sidelines ended in tragedy when a pickup truck sped onto the field, killing a 6-year-old boy and a man and injuring 10 others. The truck had been parked in a space near the soccer fields at Stryker Sports Complex before it went onto one of the fields around 3:25 p.m. local time, police said. The driver, a 34-year-old woman, was released “pending the results of toxicology testing and a mechanical examination of her vehicle” after investigators conducted interviews with witnesses and consulted with the district attorney’s office, according to a news release from the Wichita Police Department. Two of the woman’s children were with her in the truck and another was playing soccer on a different field at the complex, according to police. Officials are still working to determine more about what happened and why. Police said Saturday evening that the woman had been cooperative in the investigation. Charges have not been filed at this time, officials said. The 10 people injured ranged in age from 5 to 68, including five children, police said. They had injuries ranging from bruises to extremely severe injuries, though none appeared to be life-threatening. The victims who died were identified as 6-year-old Cole Adrian and 35-year-old Nicholas Schafer, police said. Police originally misidentified the 6-year-old in a release, reversing his first and last name. An 11th person was also taken to a local hospital after experiencing medical complications unrelated to traumatic injuries, police said. “This is a tragedy,” Aaron Moses with the Wichita Police Department told reporters outside the complex. First responders arrived on scene to find community members providing medical aid to those who were injured, Moses said. ‘It was pure panic’ Children were playing soccer on the field with their families gathered nearby when the screeching sound of tires rang out, a video obtained by CNN shows. The camera of the woman filming the video shakes as she flees the area, with her and others’ screams audible in the recording that appears to capture the moment the truck entered the field. Vanessa Trammell, who was at the complex watching her 13-year-old son’s soccer game nearby, saw the truck drive across the neighboring field near the sidelines, striking several people, she told CNN. “It was pure panic,” Trammell said. “I didn’t know what was going on – just that people were being hit. I’m pretty sure I probably screamed, but, absolutely, just pure panic was going through me.” She added her son’s coach ran to help victims before paramedics arrived at the scene. One youth player, identified by CNN affiliate KWCH only as Isaac, told the outlet his father was one of the people who rushed to remove the driver from the vehicle. “My dad went to the truck (and) took the person out of the truck so that they don’t hit any more people,” Isaac said. “(I’m) shocked he did that cause if he didn’t do that, maybe the car wouldn’t have stopped and more people could’ve gotten hit.” View from outside the Stryker Sports Complex, on October 17, 2026. - KWCH-DT Dozens of first responders quickly swarmed the scene, as children wearing their red sports uniforms gathered near the emergency vehicles, video shows. The driver and two juveniles were still with the vehicle when officers and paramedics arrived, Moses said. It’s unclear how fast the vehicle was going or how it breached the Stryker Sports Complex, which is fenced off and has a concrete runway leading to the parking lot, Moses said. The complex hosts recreational and competitive youth soccer leagues for players ranging from under-5 age groups through high school, as well as adult leagues, according to its website . It has 11 outdoor turf fields and an indoor facility. Investigators have interviewed more than 30 witnesses at the scene and others over the phone, and have asked for the public’s help as they search for video from the sports complex, Moses said. All events at the complex have been canceled until further notice, the facility said. Flag football state championship games scheduled at an adjacent field have also been suspended as police probe the scene, the Kansas State High School Activities Association said in a statement. Wichita Mayor Lily Wu said she’s “heartbroken” and advised people to avoid the area. “My heart breaks for the families who have lost loved ones, especially the family grieving the loss of a child,” the mayor said. This story has been updated with additional information. CNN’s Maria Aguilar, Taylor Galgano, Sarah Dewberry and Diego Mendoza contributed to this report. articles.title: U.S. resumes intelligence-sharing with Ukraine after pause, Zelensky says
articles.summary: Oct 18 (Reuters) - The United States has resumed providing Ukraine critical intelligence to help it defend against Russian missile strikes, after a brief pause, Ukrainian President ‌Volodymyr Zelenskiy said in comments published on Sunday. Ukraine has relied on US intelligence ‌to spot the fast-moving ballistic missiles that Russia has fired in waves at its cities. US President Donald Trump ​had said earlier this week that Washington was still sharing intelligence, although Ukrainian officials said some Russian strikes had occurred without warning. Speaking to NBC's Meet the Press, Zelenskiy said intelligence-sharing had been interrupted but later "de-blocked." "We are very thankful for this," he said. "Now it works." But Zelenskiy said other US actions, ‌such as signing a deal ⁠to import Russian diesel and waiving sanctions on Russia that had been slated to take effect this week, will hurt Ukraine. "If the United States ⁠will officially take the side of Russia, of course if these two countries will be together, of course we will not prevail and we will not be able to stand," he said. Over ​the past ​week, a widening rift between Trump and Zelenskiy has sparked ​concerns that their tumultuous relationship could lead ‌to even worse outcomes for Kyiv. Zelenskiy told NBC that he hopes Trump will remain an ally of Ukraine. "We want to trust him, and I hope that he will change his decisions," Zelenskiy said. "Because I think that it's all mistakes and it will not help us. And it will not help United States." In a Truth Social post on Sunday afternoon, Trump wrote ‌that his decision-making was aimed at avoiding anything "that ​will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table." Ukraine ​gets US help that Russia does not ​receive, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told NBC, citing intelligence-sharing and the ‌provision of US munitions to other countries ​for resale to Ukraine. But Bessent, ​speaking with "Meet the Press" after it aired Zelenskiy's interview, did not directly answer when asked multiple times whether the United States views Ukraine as an ally. "Zelenskiy presents a ​false binary this morning that ‌Ukraine must win," Bessent said. "The war must end, and that will be with ​some kind of a negotiated settlement." (Reporting by Dan Peleschuk and Michael Derby; Editing ​by Joe Bavier, Sergio Non and Edmund Klamann) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/us-resumes-intelligence-sharing-ukraine-135650691.html

articles.title: Rubio says Trump will take up to 60 days to weigh Russia sanctions
articles.summary: By Nandita Bose and Gram Slattery Oct 17 (Reuters) - The day after waiving sanctions and tariffs related to Russian exports, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter, ‌while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials want more time to evaluate the situation. Rubio said on Saturday that ‌the president will use up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs that he waived a day earlier. "A lot of you don't ​know what my decision is yet, but we'll figure it out, and you'll figure it out," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. In a Truth Social post on Sunday, Trump wrote that his decision-making was aimed at avoiding anything "that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table." Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions and tariffs under the law known as the Graham ‌Act, which he signed last month at ⁠the urging of lawmakers who want to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine. The measures, including tariffs on Russian goods and penalties on countries buying Russian oil and gas, were due to take effect next ⁠week. Friday's order did not specify how long the waiver would last, but Rubio said Trump opted for a 60-day review. "I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and ​even to ​the US economy," Rubio told reporters before boarding a plane for a trip ​to Uzbekistan. Friday's executive order drew criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, ‌who warned it would embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war. DIESEL SUPPLIES Rubio on Saturday also defended a separate US agreement with Russia to increase diesel supplies to global markets, aimed at easing fuel prices that have climbed amid the war with Iran and disruptions to energy supplies. "That diesel is going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio said. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get." Under the agreement, Trump said Russia initially would supply more than 300,000 metric tons of ‌diesel to the United States, followed by shipments in November and beyond. The ​diesel agreement is "a carrot to try to end the war, not an economic lifeline" ​to Russia, US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said ​during a Sunday interview on ABC's "This Week." But "the only way they can get additional diesel to export is ‌if they turn down the conflict with Ukraine," Wright told ​CNN's "State of the Union" program ​on Sunday. “If Russia can bring additional diesel to the market and export it, it would benefit American consumers,” he told CNN. “He's putting pressure that would both benefit American consumers and be a step forward for peace in the Russia-Ukraine war.” Rubio said ​the diesel deal and sanctions waiver reflected ‌the challenge of managing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine that have disrupted global energy supplies. "These conflicts around ​the world are starting to crash into each other," he said. (Reporting by Nandita Bose in Kentucky, Gram Slattery in ​Washington and Doyinsola Oladipo; Editing by Sergio Non and Christopher Cushing) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/rubio-says-trump-60-days-033841652.html

articles.title: 'It's like a war zone': Fresh clashes break out in Paris after historic day of unrest
articles.summary: By Sybille de La Hamaide, Clotaire Achi and Abdul Saboor PARIS/LIMOGES, Oct 18 (Reuters) - President Emmanuel Macron appealed for calm on Sunday, a day after France suffered one of its worst days of unrest in years, with thousands arrested and shops looted or damaged after protests over high prices and declining public services. Fresh ‌clashes broke out in Paris and Marseille, where riot police intervened to prevent attempts to ransack businesses. Nationwide demonstrations had erupted into riots on Saturday, with a town ‌hall torched, shops pillaged and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country. "Looking at these images, we have all asked ourselves: What was going through their minds? How can French people do ​this to France?" Macron said in a televised address to the nation. "Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it. Tonight, we all feel anger and shame." Saturday's unrest laid bare the deep anger at Macron, who leaves office in 2027 after a decade in power that has increasingly become defined by social discontent, a weak economy and ballooning debt. Macron said those protesting peacefully had legitimate  grievances and their actions should not be confused with those seeking to wreak havoc. He stopped short of declaring a state of emergency, as demanded by some right-wing politicians, but said the government would act to ‌allow prefects to ban protests if necessary to protect public buildings ⁠and local businesses. PARIS PROTESTS 'LIKE A WAR ZONE' The government has blamed the violence on what it said were ultra-left groups, as well as criminals it said had instigated the looting. One protester died on Saturday after suffering a cardiac arrest during demonstrations in Paris. Police made 2,400 arrests across France, ⁠while nearly 1,000 officers were injured, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said. Police again clashed with protesters and fired tear gas at Place de la Republique on Sunday afternoon, and protesters had set fire to piles of bicycles. A Reuters witness said there appeared to be several hundred protesters in the area. A massive clean-up operation took place in cities from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south and ​from ​Strasbourg in the east to Bordeaux in the southwest, where a masked mob invaded the residence of the ​local prefect. "It's like a war zone here!" exclaimed Dutch entrepreneur Tije De ‌Boer, who was visiting Paris with his children and said the unrest forced him to evacuate his hotel at Place de la Republique. More than half a million people joined marches in scores of cities on Saturday, marking the convergence of a month-long student movement with broader social discontent against rising living costs and declining public services. SEVERAL HUNDRED SHOPS DAMAGED While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully across France on Saturday, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers. Far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen, frontrunner going into next year's presidential campaign, also called for calm, saying France must not become accustomed to images of the country being battered, abused and ransacked. "Violence is not an opinion. Destruction is not a ‌form of expression. And chaos cannot serve as a project for France," she said in a video address. Hard-left ​France Unbowed presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon said Macron needed to answer the demands of protesting high-school students. In Limoges, ​famed for its porcelain, the collapse of the town hall's clock tower in a ​fiery blaze revived memories of the 2019 fire that devastated Paris' Notre Dame cathedral. Mayor Guillaume Guerin said not enough officers from the national police ‌had been deployed to his city. "There was a clear, premeditated intention to ​burn down the town hall, and the people ​inside feared for their lives," Guerin told Reuters on Sunday. He threatened to resign if the city did not receive the funds needed to repair the town hall. Economy Minister Roland Lescure pledged support on Sunday for business owners who suffered losses. "Those who break things will pay, repair the damage and be held accountable for their intention to ​sow chaos," Lescure said in a statement. French retailer Carrefour's CEO Alexandre ‌Bompard told French broadcaster BFMTV that 50 of the company's shops had been damaged, including 20 that were looted, with losses from the damage running into ​the tens of millions of euros. (Reporting by Sybille de La Hamaide, Janis Laizans, Abdul Saboor, Clotaire Achi, Marc Leras, Michel Rose, Elizabeth Pineau, Natasa Bansagi; Writing ​by Sybille de la Hamaide; Editing by Richard Lough, Elaine Hardcastle, Jan Harvey and Edmund Klamann) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.news.yahoo.com/france-faces-aftermath-worst-unrest-094920368.html

articles.title: Trump endorses Netanyahu just 9 days before Israeli elections
articles.summary: The relationship between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin and US President Donald Trump, shown in April, 2025, has soured ahead of crucial elections. - Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images/FILE With just over a week to go until Israel’s election day, President Donald Trump finally gave the full-throated endorsement that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had long sought. The president called Netanyahu a “Great Warrior Prime Minister” in a post on social media, which he said serves as his “Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu.” Trump also hinted at a possible resumption of hostilities in the unpopular war with Iran — a war the US launched alongside Israel eight months ago — saying that if the Iranians do not “change their ways, rapidly, we will soon finish the job.” Netanyahu was quick to respond, thanking Trump for the “tremendous support and the joint work.” Trump told Axios journalist and CNN Global Affairs analyst Barak Ravid in a brief phone interview that he had always intended to endorse Netanyahu. “I was always going to do that. I just didn’t want to do it too soon,” he said. Trump added that they have a “good relationship” and would “continue to do well” together if Netanyahu is reelected, according to Ravid. “It is important that Israel has a person they can count on,” Trump said. It was an endorsement that seemed uncertain until it finally arrived and cannot mask what has become at times a rocky relationship between the two. For years, Israelis driving the country’s highways in the final weeks of an election have seen the same image: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu standing beside President Donald Trump, under the slogan, “A different league.” Less than two weeks before the October 27 vote, the billboards of Netanyahu are back. But this time Trump is not on them. The president still appears in some videos for Netanyahu’s Likud party, but his absence may signal something beyond advertising. Until Sunday, Trump had held off endorsing Netanyahu. “I’m not involved in [Israeli] politics anymore,” he told Time earlier this month. On Thursday, Trump told Newsmax that Netanyahu would like him to be involved in the election. “I’ve had a very good relationship with him,” he said, but avoided endorsing him again. When asked directly whether he trusts Netanyahu, he said bluntly, “I don’t trust anybody in the world of politics.” Trump has starred in Netanyahu’s campaigns since 2013, when still a businessman and TV personality, he released a video urging Israelis to “vote for Benjamin.” When Trump entered the White House in 2017, he showered Netanyahu with political gifts. About two weeks before Israel’s April 2019 election, Netanyahu was in Washington to watch Trump sign a historic proclamation recognizing Israeli sovereignty over the occupied Golan Heights. In January 2020, five weeks before Israelis went again to the polls, Trump unveiled the Israeli-Palestinian “Deal of the Century” plan. Netanyahu stood smiling by his side. Ahead of this election, there has been no red carpet. The last time Netanyahu and Trump met at the White House in August, there were no cameras. The two did not meet at all when Netanyahu traveled to New York for the UN General Assembly in September. Demonstrators protest against Netanyahu's address to the UN General Assembly in New York in September. His efforts to undercut peace talks have drawn bipartisan ire. - David Dee Delgado/Reuters A protesters against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's policies is arrested after blocking a street next to the United Nations. - Spencer Platt/Getty Images Over the course of the last year, Netanyahu has taken steps that have drawn fury from Trump, including undermining Trump-led peace efforts by striking inside Lebanon and Gaza. Trump has cursed the prime minister out in phone calls and warned him he’s losing support among Americans, according to people familiar with the conversations. He’s asked why Israel was blowing up apartment buildings in Lebanon and warned about the risk of a global economic downturn as a result of the Iran war. Inside the White House, many of the moves were interpreted as election-year posturing by Netanyahu, whose internal politics are well known by Trump and his advisers. Over the summer, many Trump advisers came to the conclusion that Netanyahu was trying to prolong the Iran war to bolster his own political standing. Trump has given Netanyahu a degree of leeway because of those political concerns, people familiar with the matter said. But he’s still grown frustrated at some of Israel’s actions, many of which he believes run counter to American interests. Another person close to Trump suggested his lack of endorsement had been tied to Netanyahu’s weakness in the polls. Trump has long been careful to avoid endorsing candidates who seem likely to lose. In conversations over the past several months, Trump has quizzed Netanyahu about the election and his prospects, according to people familiar with the matter. While Netanyahu has sought to project confidence, Trump is well aware of the prime minister’s difficult political position. As Netanyahu’s standing fell in the Trump administration, so did Trump’s standing in Israel. According to Israeli sources close to Netanyahu, Trump was originally meant to be a centerpiece of Netanyahu’s campaign. Last December, at Mar-a-Lago, the prime minister announced that Trump would become the first non-Israeli to receive the prestigious Israel Prize. Netanyahu aides hoped Trump would accept the prize in person at Israel’s Independence Day ceremony in April, giving jumpstarting the campaign. Then came the war with Iran. A smoke plume rises following a missile strike on a building in Tehran on March 1, 2026. - Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty Images The joint US-Israeli attack began on February 28 with the two leaders projecting strategic harmony. Netanyahu thanked “my friend, President Donald Trump,” calling him “a leader who stands by his word.” Trump described the two of them as “war heroes” and publicly demanded that Israel’s president grant Netanyahu a pardon in his ongoing corruption trials. But Trump never showed interest in attending the Israel Prize ceremony. By then, the fighting in Iran had ended and ceasefire talks were underway. The Iran ceasefire and subsequent memorandum of understanding were deeply unpopular in Israel, particularly on the right. Yinon Magal, a pro-Netanyahu TV anchor, called Trump a “loser” after the deal was signed. A July survey by the Jewish People Policy Institute found that only 7% of Israelis had “a great deal of trust” that Trump “will do the right thing” on US-Israel relations, and 45% had none. “Trump’s stock in Israel, especially among right wing-voters, has weakened,” a Likud source said. “An endorsement would not necessarily have helped Netanyahu so much, so he did not invest much in it.” Another Likud source said, “It’s not as if Trump will endorse any other opponent, so it’s nice to have, but not a must.” US President Donald Trump leaves the stage after speaking during a campaign rally at the Freeman Coliseum on October 07, in San Antonio, Texas. - Win McNamee/Getty Images Netanyahu’s opponents are watching, but with less alarm than before. “A year ago, our camp was calling anyone close to Trump to prevent an endorsement,” one senior opposition figure said ahead of Sunday’s news. “Now it doesn’t really matter, the charm is not there.” When Trump was asked specifically about who is currently polling as Netanyahu’s leading challenger, he said, “Well, I don’t know, I don’t hear bad things about him.” He then said, “They’ve written Bibi off many, many times, just like they’ve written me off many, many times. I wouldn’t underestimate Bibi.” Trump has his own reasons for distance. American public opinion of Israel has fallen sharply, declining even more against the backdrop of the Iran war. Israel’s average net favorability fell from +51 points in July 2018 to -16 in July 2026, according to multiple polls, a 67-point drop over eight years. As America quickly soured on the Iran war, a source familiar with the relationship said, Trump has been “trying to shed the image that Netanyahu pulled him into it.” Still, the apparent distance may be misleading. Israeli sources say the two leaders have recently discussed renewed strikes on Iran. Israeli security sources told CNN preparations are underway - pending Trump’s decision - with timing unclear because of the US midterm elections. Netanyahu rejected suggestions he was seeking escalation before the vote. “It is not convenient for us, it’s no good,” he told Army Radio this week. He complained that if Iran fired missiles at Israel, his opponents “will blame me.” For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/18/world/trump-netanyahu-elections-relations-intl

articles.title: Coastal storm threatens East Coast with high winds and flooding
articles.summary: A slow-moving coastal storm is expected to bring high winds, flooding and dangerous surf to parts of the East Coast this week, with forecasters also monitoring the system for possible subtropical development. The National Hurricane Center (NHC) said Sunday that a storm-force non- tropical low was expected to form off the Southeast coast on Sunday or Sunday night and move “slowly and erratically” through the middle of the week. The agency gave the system a near-zero chance of development within 48 hours and a 30 percent chance within seven days. “Regardless of development, this system will cause high winds, coastal flooding, and dangerous surf along portions of the U.S. East Coast,” the NHC said. If it develops into a named subtropical or tropical storm , it would be called Josephine, according to the list of next named storms. The possibility comes during an unusually quiet Atlantic hurricane season. Through October 18, the basin had produced nine named storms but only one hurricane, Isaias, which is currently the year’s only major Atlantic hurricane. Forecasters say the storm does not need to become Josephine to produce significant coastal impacts. “AccuWeather hurricane experts continue to monitor a medium risk for tropical or subtropical development off the East Coast between October 19th and October 23rd,” Alexander Duffus, a meteorologist for forecasting operations with AccuWeather, told Newsweek in an email Sunday. Duffus added: “Regardless of if this will eventually be designated as a subtropical or tropical storm by the National Hurricane Center in the coming days, gusty winds, rough surf, beach erosion and coastal flooding can be expected for portions of the mid-Atlantic through early to the middle of this week.” A storm in the Atlantic has 30 percent chance of development over the next seven days, according to the National Hurricane Center. East Coast Threats The most prolonged effects are expected from the Delmarva Peninsula into eastern North Carolina , with rain, gusty winds, beach erosion and coastal flooding among the threats, according to The Weather Channel. High surf and dangerous rip currents could extend much farther, from Florida to New England . AccuWeather said the most significant coastal impacts could occur around the Outer Banks of North Carolina, southeastern Virginia and the beach communities of Maryland and Delaware . “The coastal hazards risk at this time is greatest from coastal New Jersey to the Outer Banks of North Carolina through Tuesday,” Duffus said. “Very wind[y] conditions are expected with gusts from 40-60 mph that can blow around unsecured objects. Coastal flooding and beach erosion can also occur, especially during high tide cycles. Coastal Flooding and Beach Erosion The storm’s slow movement could prolong its effects on vulnerable beaches and coastal communities. The Weather Channel reported that the system could remain offshore for days, producing high surf, rip currents, coastal flooding, rain and strong winds. The outlet said the storm was not expected to be as strong as the late-September nor’easter but could linger through much of the week. AccuWeather similarly forecast long-duration gusty winds, beach erosion and tidal flooding, with the Outer Banks and southeastern Virginia potentially seeing greater impacts than areas farther north because of the storm’s expected position and duration. The National Weather Service’s Eastern Region coastal hazard page showed a range of active coastal and marine hazards Sunday, including coastal flood, high surf and gale alerts in parts of the region. A strong non-tropical low pressure area is expected to form during the next day or two off of the eastern coast of the U.S. This low is likely to move slowly and erratically through the middle of next week, and some subtropical development is possible during this time. articles.title: Jackson doesn't regret telling Collins to 'shut up' after protester interrupted debate
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Maine Democrat Troy Jackson says he does not regret telling Sen. Susan Collins that she should “shut up” after the Republican suggested a protester who interrupted their recent debate was one of his campaign's backers. "She said that it was a Troy supporter. She accused me of setting that up. I had no idea who it was,” said Jackson, a former president of the state Senate who is trying to deny Collins, the longest-serving Republican woman in Senate history, a sixth-term. He spoke in an interview with CNN’s “State of the Union” that aired Sunday. During their final debate Thursday night in the closely contested race, as the Nov. 3 election nears a protester opposing data centers began yelling as Collins spoke. While moderators asked for that person to be removed, the senator said the demonstrator was “obviously one of Troy’s supporters.” Jackson responded: “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.” The Sunrise Movement group posted on its Instagram page that the outburst came from one of its members. In a caption of an Instagram post, the group's page said: “We’re proud of this Sunrise volunteer who took action yesterday.” The New York Times said the protester, Henry Elgie, a 19-year-old student at Bowdoin College in Maine, told the newspaper in an interview Saturday that he had “zero coordination” with Jackson's campaign. "I do not know Troy Jackson personally or at all,” he was quoted as saying. The Sunrise Movement is a left-wing political advocacy organization that champions the Green New Deal, aimed at transitioning the U.S. economy to 100% renewable energy. The group, which has local arms around the country, regularly organizes protests, sit-ins and climate strikes. Jackson told CNN that he shook hands with Collins after each of their debates. “But what I’m not going to be is talked down to by Sen. Collins,” he said. He added: "I’m fighting for Mainers and I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me and I’m not going to apologize for that.” Collins told Fox News’ Sean Hannity on Friday that she was “struck by how reflective the response, ‘Oh, shut up,’ was.” Collins said "the fact that it seemed like such an automatic, quick reply was very telling.” She cited what she said was “the reputation” that Jackson had in the Legislature “particularly when he’s dealing with women with whom he disagrees. So in some ways it didn’t surprise me.” Some state lawmakers who worked with Jackson have criticized him as having a temper, including once throwing a plastic water bottle on the ground in frustration while disagreeing with a female lawmaker. Asked by reporters during the campaign about the confrontations, Jackson said, "I wear my heart on my sleeve.” He took responsibility for his outburst and apologized to those he had confrontations with at the time. Jackson was asked on CNN about some Republicans who are saying there were stories that he was aggressive in his tone to women from his time in the Legislature and that his remark Thursday night was another example of that. Jackson said some Republicans have been spending millions “attacking me and my family, making untrue claims. … So it doesn’t surprise me." articles.title: A timeline of the Cornell rape case, from the alleged 2024 incident to the frat party ban
articles.summary: The investigation into an alleged "gang rape" at Cornell University in October 2024 has drawn nationwide attention after a former student identified as "Jane Doe" filed a civil lawsuit last month, accusing seven fraternity members of drugging and assaulting her for hours. Last week, Cornell announced that it is suspending "all parties and social events" at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year while an independent review is underway. "These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue," Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff wrote in a letter to the Cornell community . Kotlikoff also announced that the university would enlist "experienced, trauma-informed criminal investigators" to investigate allegations of sexual assault on its Ithaca, N.Y., campus. Earlier this month, Cornell's board of trustees announced it had retained former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates, a partner at law firm King & Spalding, to lead an outside review of how the university responds to sexual assault. Separately, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as the special prosecutor to oversee the criminal investigation after losing faith in both Cornell and Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who initially declined to bring charges in the Jane Doe case. "This young woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable," the governor said. "And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her." All of the men identified in Jane Doe's civil suit have denied any wrongdoing, according to the New York Times . None has been charged with a crime. On Friday, a New York judge denied a request from one of the accused fraternity members for a gag order in Jane Doe’s civil case. Here is a timeline of the case, from the alleged incident to the reopening of a criminal investigation, culled from Jane Doe's civil lawsuit, statements from Cornell and public officials, and other reports. August 2022 "Jane Doe" begins her freshman year at Cornell University, where she joins a sorority, Tri-Delta's Alpha Beta Chapter. Oct. 19-20, 2024 Jane Doe drinks vodka at her residence at the sorority before attending a Tri-Delta event hosted at Moonies Bar and Nightclub, where she is allegedly served alcohol despite identifying herself as underage. Around 11 p.m., Jane Doe walks to the Chi Phi fraternity house, arriving "visibly intoxicated" after consuming "about 10 standard drinks within the past 3 hours," according to her civil lawsuit. Shortly after arriving, Jane Doe is allegedly pressured by two fraternity brothers into snorting what they said was ketamine before taking part in a threesome proposed by the men. "In her drunken state, Plaintiff was incapable of consenting to this proposition," the lawsuit alleges. At 1:41 a.m., one of the men sends a message to the fraternity's Snapchat group suggesting that she was available for sex, according to the lawsuit, which included a screengrab of part of the group chat. The complaint alleges that multiple fraternity members show up and rape her over several hours. During the alleged assault, the fraternity members begin "pouring lines of Ketamine all over her body and snorting them," per the complaint. At around 5:45 a.m., the alleged assault ends and Jane Doe loses consciousness, her lawsuit states. Later that day, Jane Doe returns to the sorority house "in a state of shock," per her suit. Oct. 21, 2024 Jane Doe exchanges text messages with one of the men she would later name in the lawsuit, who tells her, "I just wanted to apologize for how things went down the other night," according to the New York Times . She replies: "At the end of the day non of the sexual stuff was illegal and honestly i really liked being w u and matt." Oct. 22, 2024 Jane Doe makes an appointment at Cornell Health for a urinary tract infection and wants to be tested for sexually transmitted diseases, telling the doctor she contracted it "in a traumatic way," per the Times. The doctor doesn't follow up and suggests she "go to therapy." Oct. 23, 2024 In another text exchange, Jane Doe tells one of the fraternity members that "my reputation is destroyed and I'm utterly ashamed," according to ABC News . In the same exchange, she also says: "everyone needs to grow up because sexuality and sex and [stuff] is changing and stuff like this is going to become more common. i'm also really open minded tho. i love u king." Oct. 30, 2024 Jane Doe sends a text to the same frat member saying she was "uninvited" to an upcoming Chi Phi Halloween party. "i knew this was going to happen. the woman will always get the short end of the stick," she writes. "yall aren't my friends. yall are covering your a****." Nov. 7, 2024 In a recorded phone call with one of the fraternity members, Jane Doe says she was "10 shots deep" when she arrived at the Chi Phi fraternity house and is now struggling to remember what happened, according to audio obtained by ABC News. The fraternity member insists Jane Doe told him she was sober before the alleged encounter, which she denies. At one point during the call, Jane Doe tells him, "If I wanted to take this somewhere, what y'all did would be classified as gang rape." The fraternity member then suggests that their memory of what transpired may be inaccurate. Jane Doe pushes back: "No, because I remember looking up and being like, 'That is too many people.'" Nov. 8, 2024 Jane Doe reports the Oct. 19-20 incident to campus police. Nov. 14, 2024 According to CBS News , Jane Doe gives an interview to campus police in which she states: "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped." (Van Houten later says his office was not provided with a transcript of that interview when it decided not to pursue charges.) Nov. 15, 2024 Jane Doe gives a sworn statement to campus police in which she says that the incident "felt like coercion," according to ABC News . She recalls that at one point, she said "no to the foursome" that one of the fraternity brothers had proposed. She also states: "I remember being totally disgusted at the situation, and I felt very tired and intoxicated. I would say that my level of overall intoxication was about a 8 out of 10 level of intoxicated. I would say that it was the most intoxicated I've ever been in my life. I felt like I was unable to make any decision because of how intoxicated I was." Nov. 26, 2024 Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff publishes an open letter to students and alumni with an update on the "ongoing investigations into the serious and deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house." He says that "interim measures in the form of temporary suspensions were issued for a number of students to protect the immediate physical health and safety of all students." "The behavior that has been outlined in the many allegations received is abhorrent and cannot be tolerated within our community. I urge anyone who has experienced or is aware of sexual misconduct on our campus to report it," he adds. "Only those who perpetrate sexual violence benefit from its concealment." Jan. 14, 2025 Cornell commences a Title IX investigation in response to Jane Doe's allegations, according to her lawsuit, holding at least 12 hearings over a four-week period in May. According to ABC News , Jane Doe tells the school's investigators that she "felt like bait" on the night of the alleged assault. "I felt like lions around me," she says during one of the hearings. The comments are included in a 99-page report prepared in August by the university as part of its Title IX investigation, per ABC. The report also includes comments from a fraternity member who Cornell's investigation later concluded did not engage in the assault but was found responsible for "attempted sexual exploitation." "I was sorry that maybe if it wasn't consensual and she was victimized, I was sorry for not stopping it," the fraternity member says, according to ABC. According to the New York Times , Jane Doe tells Cornell's Title IX investigators that she did not consider herself a victim until she saw the incident being discussed as a "gang rape" in an online forum. "That's the first time I had ever heard the narrative change that I wasn't a whore and that I was assaulted," Jane Doe tells investigators, per the Times. Feb. 6, 2025 Cornell establishes a Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault that is "charged with understanding and addressing sexual assault involving undergraduate students on the Ithaca campus." March 10, 2026 Cornell University releases the task force's final report with recommendations aimed at "developing a holistic public health framework for addressing sexual assault": "By improving communication, education, transparency, and access to resources, we can ensure students are well-informed and supported as we work to confront sexual assault at Cornell," the school says . "Among the key measures in the report are launching a public health campaign; increasing students' knowledge and clarity of reporting options and confidential resources; developing new educational opportunities, including courses focused on sexual citizenship; prioritizing evidence‑based prevention strategies; and expanding training for students, leaders, and residential staff." Sept. 16, 2026 Jane Doe files a civil lawsuit in New York State Supreme Court against Cornell University, seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity, the Chi Phi and Tri-Delta Alpha Beta House chapters and the owners of Moonies Bar & Nightclub. Sept. 21, 2026 Cornell University releases a statement saying it is aware of "a lawsuit concerning the deeply disturbing allegations of sexual assault involving members of the student community that occurred in 2024." The university says that it "adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies," adding: "Federal privacy law prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students and we therefore are unable to make a public statement on any other disciplinary response." Sept. 28, 2026 Van Houten, the Tompkins County district attorney, announces that he has reopened a criminal investigation into the alleged incident. Van Houten describes the allegations as "morally disturbing," but argues that the facts he knew at the time did not support a prosecution. "My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later," Van Houten says in a lengthy statement that sought to explain why he initially decided not to prosecute the case. Cornell releases a statement saying it supports the district attorney's decision to reopen the case, while pushing back against critics who say it did not "impose consequential punishments for those involved." "The complainant and respondents had the opportunity to testify and present evidence," the school says. "At its conclusion, the hearing panel issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell. None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement." Oct. 1, 2026 Hochul says she has lost faith in Van Houten and signs an executive order appointing New York Attorney General Letitia James as the special prosecutor to oversee the investigation. Oct. 2, 2026 Hochul holds a press conference with James to explain her appointment as special prosecutor, saying Jane Doe was "failed" by people obligated to protect her. "In what world would the police learn from a victim that she'd been literally gang raped while intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney?" Hochul says. "In what world does the district attorney not even interview her or anyone else involved or even request the full transcript?" James says that the case is "now an active criminal investigation." "We will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses and, if warranted, pursue prosecutions," she says, adding: "I know that you want answers. I do too." Oct. 3, 2026 Kotlikoff, Cornell's president, posts an eight-minute video statement , saying it "has been one of the most difficult weeks" in the university's history, and that the school "must do better" to address sexual assault and substance abuse on campus. "What happened to Jane Doe in 2024 is deeply disturbing and will weigh heavily on our community for years to come. My heart aches when I think of what she experienced," Kotlikoff says. "It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use. It also raises questions around the investigations conducted after the allegations were reported." Oct. 4, 2026 Jane Doe's attorney, Thomas Giuffra, says his client has received "multiple threats" in recent days from people who want her to withdraw her lawsuit. "There are people out there trying to track her down," Giuffra says on CNN's State of the Union . "They said, 'We're gonna shut you up. You're gonna still get hurt by us.'" Oct. 5, 2026 Thousands of people gather at Cornell for a protest against the university's handling of sexual assault cases. The "Justice for Survivors" rally takes place in front of Day Hall, which houses the university's administrative offices and had been vandalized by activists overnight. "We are known as the rape school," Saya Taylor, a Cornell sophomore, says at the event. "We can be known as leading a nationwide reform movement." Kotlikoff and Ryan Lombardi, the school's vice president for student and campus life, meet with the Graduate and Professional Student Assembly, which presses them on their response to Jane Doe's allegations. "We're all angry. I understand that anger," Kotlikoff says, according to the Cornell Daily Sun . "People want easy answers to this." Oct. 6, 2026 Cornell's board of trustees announces it has retained former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates, a partner at law firm King & Spalding, to lead an independent review of how the university responds to sexual assault on campus. Oct. 13, 2026 Cornell imposes a ban on all fraternity parties and social events for the remainder of the 2026-2027 academic year. Kotlikoff, Cornell's president, also announces that the university will enlist "experienced, trauma-informed criminal investigators" to review allegations of sexual assault on campus. "These are first steps toward systemic change," Kotlikoff writes in a letter to the Cornell community . "We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe's experiences, and those of other survivors. Cornell must be a place where safety is not an open question." In an interview with the New York Times , Kotlikoff says he learned of Jane Doe's allegations shortly after she reported them to campus police, but did not follow up with her or seek to determine whether the fraternity members she accused had been punished. He also says he was not informed when Van Houten, the local prosecutor, declined to bring charges and was unaware that Jane Doe had dropped out of Cornell until last month, when she filed suit. "The fact that Jane Doe experienced what she experienced at Cornell is something that I am personally sorry for," Kotlikoff says. "And I think this entire campus is sorry that occurred." Oct. 14, 2026 In a " heated " meeting, Kotlikoff is pressed by " angry " faculty members over the university's handling of the Jane Doe case. The meeting is held as the faculty senate is considering a no-confidence resolution to condemn the school's response to sexual violence on campus. A vote on the resolution is expected at the end of the month. Oct. 16, 2026 A New York judge denies a request from one of the accused fraternity members for a gag order limiting what lawyers and parties in Jane Doe’s civil lawsuit can say publicly. Judge Phaedra Perry-Bond calls the dispute a “side show,” according to ABC News . Lawyers for two of the accused students also continue pressing for James to be removed as special prosecutor, pointing to a social media post in which she expressed support for Jane Doe. Hochul has said she stands by the appointment. The same day, students hold a mock trial outside a Cornell Board of Trustees meeting, “convicting” the fraternity system, Kotlikoff and several administrators in protest of the university’s handling of the case. This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/article/a-timeline-of-the-cornell-rape-case-from-the-alleged-2024-incident-to-the-ban-of-frat-parties-on-campus-192527196.html

articles.title: Trump's D.C. golf course overhaul will close popular links for 15 months
articles.summary: Topline East Potomac Golf Links, a highly popular municipal golf course in Washington, D.C., and the target of one of President Donald Trump’s contentious renovation projects, will close for 15 months starting in November, the president said on Sunday. An aerial view of the East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, D.C. taken in May 2026. Getty Images Key Facts In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump shared a map of the redesigned course, which he said would be “open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments.” The “current Course” will close when renovations begin on Nov. 15, Trump said, and will reopen in “approximately 15 months.” The announcement comes shortly after the National Park Service cut down hundreds of trees at the course, a move that prompted a federal judge to block further tree removal and chastise lawyers for the Trump administration. Big Number 430. That’s how many healthy, non-invasive trees were removed from the East Potomac Golf Links in a few hours last week, the Trump administration acknowledged. “Breakneck speed to clear trees that posed no harm,” District Court Judge Ana Reyes wrote in a memo accompanying an order to stop cutting down any tree at the course until Oct. 26. “The reason? Disputed. The budget? Unclear. The environmental impact? Unstudied. The urgency? None. Next steps: bulldoze hundreds more.” Contra Days after the order was signed, the Trump administration moved to disqualify Reyes from presiding over the case, claiming she “hamstrung the Government’s legitimate attempts to maintain East Potomac Park” and accused her of being biased against the Trump administration. “More than being upset and furious right now, I am just deeply disappointed in the government,” Reyes reportedly told Justice Department lawyers at a hearing. When one attorney told the judge the government had done its best to gather information about the tree removal project, Reyes reportedly responded with: “You did not do your best. You did ⁠your absolute worst.” Key Background Trump previously announced work would begin on renovating the golf course in September. The current course has two nine-hold courses for easier difficulty levels, one par 72 18-hole course, and a mini-golf course. Green fees max out at $48 for the 18-hole course on weekends and holidays, but the easier courses cost even less. Trump, who is an avid golfer and investor in high-end golf clubs like his Trump Doral in Miami and Trump National Golf Club in Bedminster, New Jersey, said he planned to replace the municipal course with a “championship-level” course. In his post on Sunday, Trump doubled down on this promise, writing the “United States Golf Association, PGA of America, and the PGA Tour have already been notified that they will soon have one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World to put on their list of great places to play, and hold Major Events.” During his second term in office, Trump has been increasingly concerned with renovation projects and new monuments around the national capital, including building a new White House ballroom, a triumphal arch and renovating the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. articles.title: Trump approval hits record low, handing Democrats a clear midterm edge
articles.summary: Two weeks from Election Day, Republicans face a bleak political landscape. President Donald Trump's approval rating has fallen to a new low, and support for Democrats in the race for control of Congress is rising as inflationary pressures contribute to an acrid mood among voters, according to a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll. Trump's approval among U.S. adults now stands at 33 percent, with 66 percent disapproving; 52 percent said they disapprove strongly. That approval rating is four percentage points lower than in July and eight points lower than at this point last year. It's lower than at any point in his first term. Among likely voters, Trump's approval is 38 percent, with 62 percent disapproving. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The poll also finds that, for the first time in more than a decade, Democrats are seen as more trusted to deal with the economy. In the competition for control of the House, Democrats hold an eight-point lead among registered and likely voters, an improvement for the party since The Post's July poll, when the Democratic lead was three points with registered voters. Trump is central to Republicans' struggles. In a separate question, the poll asked voters whether they would rather have a Democratic-led Congress acting as a check on Trump or a Republican one to support his agenda. By 58 percent to 39 percent, registered voters said they prefer the Democrats. That margin is roughly double what it was a year ago. The collective results of the new survey reveal an electorate that has lost faith in the president, is deeply worried about his decision to go to war with Iran, is feeling the effects of that war - especially the price of gasoline - on their pocketbooks and now has more confidence in Democrats than Republicans to deal with major issues. Today, 72 percent say the country is heading in the wrong direction, up five points since April. The new survey findings do not predict how individual House or Senate races will turn out in November. But they help to explain why Republicans are on the defensive in these final weeks, even in areas where they have traditionally held a strong advantage. Republicans still enjoy an overall lead in money to pour into political advertising that they hope will hold back the Democratic tide. Tellingly, those resources are shifting to protect some candidates in redder areas, a sign of the growing concerns among party leaders and strategists about the overall climate. As always, the question of who turns out to vote will decide how individual races go, with many of the most competitive Senate races still in the balance. Nationally, Democrats have a big advantage among those who said they're "certain to vote" or have already done so, but Republicans fare relatively well among voters who turned out in the 2024 or 2022 elections, which are also strong predictors of voting. One critical unknown is how many of Trump's 77 million voters from the 2024 election will cast ballots. Midterm turnout is always lower than in presidential years and Republicans have had a harder time turning out their supporters when Trump is not on the ballot. The poll echoes those challenges. Democratic registered voters are more likely than Republicans to say they are certain to vote or have already done so, 75 percent versus 67 percent. While 75 percent of Republicans who support the MAGA movement say they're certain to vote, that drops to 57 percent among non-MAGA Republicans (though more than a quarter of these non-MAGA Republicans said they prefer Democrats in control of the next Congress). By contrast, 79 percent of Democrats who support the Democratic Socialists of America say they are certain to vote, as do 73 percent of nonsocialist Democrats. Presidential approval has long been one of the most important indicators of how a midterm election will go. Based on history, Republicans are poised to lose seats from their narrow House majority and likely to lose control of the chamber next month. But how many is more difficult to predict because, in contrast to some past years, there are fewer swing districts. Republicans may also retain backing from voters who expressed only limited dissatisfaction with the president. The Post-ABC-Ipsos poll finds that among the 10 percent of likely voters who said they "somewhat disapprove" of Trump's performance, 58 percent prefer the Republican candidate for the House. Economic issues stand as a major threat to the GOP's hold on the House and Senate. Trump's economic approval rating has fallen to 28 percent, down from 33 percent in July, 41 percent in February and 49 percent at this point in the 2018 midterm election campaign. About 3 in 4 Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of inflation and the cost of living in the United States. By a 3-1 margin, Americans said the state of the economy is either not so good or poor. Most Republicans (53 percent) rate the economy positively compared with 9 percent of Democrats and 16 percent of independents. At this point in 2022, when President Joe Biden was in office, impressions of the economy were almost identically negative. But in a sign of how party allegiance can affect attitudes, 54 percent of Democrats then rated the economy positively, compared with 8 percent of Republicans and 16 percent of independents. Economic strains on many Americans are great enough that 48 percent say they are financially worse off than when Trump returned to office in 2025. That represents the highest percentage saying this about any president in Post-ABC polls since 1986. Among these financially stressed Americans, 78 percent favor Democrats for Congress, along with 71 percent of independents. Affordability is an issue that nearly all candidates are talking about this fall and the survey points to many areas of difficulty for families. The biggest is the cost of gasoline. In February, before Trump launched the war with Iran, 71 percent said gasoline was affordable. Today, as the war has disrupted supplies and shipping, pushing up gasoline and diesel prices significantly, perceptions have flipped, with 71 percent now saying gasoline is not affordable. Majorities also say groceries, health care and home energy are unaffordable, all up significantly since before the Iran war. Fewer than 4 in 10 said going out to dinner is affordable, down from half who said this in February. The shift against the president ripples throughout the survey. On Iran, 65 percent said it was a mistake to take military action and 68 percent disapprove of the way Trump has dealt with U.S. allies. Roughly 6 in 10 disapprove of his handling of immigration, a sharp departure from the beginning of his second term when 50 percent said they approved. A majority (56 percent) said Trump has gone too far in deporting undocumented immigrants, which compares with 48 percent in April 2025 as the deportation effort was beginning. Trump's negative ratings are boosted by significant criticism from his 2024 voters, including 23 percent who disapprove of his overall performance, 31 percent who disapprove of his management of the economy and 38 percent who disapprove of his handling of inflation. Most of these critics said they support Republicans for Congress, but they're far less certain about casting ballots this year than Trump voters who approve of him. Trump is judged harshly on several measures of his commitment to fundamental principles of democracy. At least 6 in 10 people said he is not committed to protecting freedom of the press and freedom of speech, free and fair elections, and respecting the authority of Congress or the courts. Beyond major issues, the public disapproves of the ways Trump has conducted himself in office. The poll finds that 66 percent said he is using the presidency to enrich himself, up from 56 percent last fall. Eight in 10 think it is inappropriate that he has pushed to put his name on the Kennedy Center in Washington (59 percent view this as "completely inappropriate"), and 74 percent say it's inappropriate that the federal government paid for television ads promoting Trump and his policies. Overall, 66 percent said they see Trump as "too extreme." The dissatisfaction with Trump inevitably has spilled onto a Republican Party that has been remade in his image. Registered voters said they trust Democrats over Republicans to handle the economy by 40 percent to 33 percent, the first Democratic advantage on the economy in Post-ABC polling since 2014. Voters split about evenly on this question in April and July of this year. Democrats also hold double-digit advantages on trust to handle inflation and the cost of living. Democrats are seen as more trustworthy on many issues even though 54 percent of U.S. adults have an unfavorable view of the party, perhaps because even more Americans - 63 percent - dislike the Republican Party. The Republican Party is seen as too extreme by 55 percent of U.S. adults, compared with 36 percent who see the Democratic Party that way. Americans hold negative impressions of the president's MAGA movement and of democratic socialism, which has roiled the Democratic Party this year. But the MAGA movement is seen even more negatively at 69 percent unfavorable compared with 59 percent unfavorable toward democratic socialism. One-quarter of Americans dislike both major political parties, but as often happens, these "double-haters" swing against the party in power, favoring Democrats by 58 percent to 32 percent in support for Congress. One factor boosting Democrats this fall, and another sign of how Trump's policies and performance have hurt him and his party, is a shift in the partisan leanings of Americans. The Pew Research Center's annual benchmarking survey - a comprehensive poll conducted over several months - found 47 percent of U.S. adults identified as Democrats or lean Democratic this spring, while 43 percent identified as or leaned Republican. That marked a shift from both 2025, when 46 percent of adults identified as Republicans and 45 percent as Democrats. Post-ABC-Ipsos polls are calibrated to match Pew's estimates for partisanship, and the latest poll reflects the national shift in party leanings. Read detailed results and cross tabs from the Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll . The poll was conducted online Oct. 9-13 among 2,545 U.S. adults nationwide reached through the Ipsos KnowledgePanel, an ongoing panel of U.S. households recruited by mail using random sampling methods. Overall results have a margin of error of plus or minus two percentage points. The error margin is plus or minus 2.2 points for results among 2,032 registered voters and likely voters; all registered voters were assigned a probability of voting to produce likely voter results. The sample was weighted to match population demographics, 2024 turnout/vote choice and political partisanship. - - - Graphics: President Trump's approval rating reaches record low Democrats hold eight-point advantage in national support for Congress Democratic-leaning groups more certain about voting in 2026 midterms Economic ratings similar to before 2022 midterms, far worse than in 2018 Record high say they are 'not as well off' financially as when Trump entered office More Americans see gas, staples and splurges are "unaffordable" Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-approval-hits-record-low-140856093.html

articles.title: 铜价高位震荡：是冲向历史新高，还是逆势反转？
articles.summary: 当铜价站上14600美元/吨，距离历史新高只差1.7%，市场开始出现"冲向新高还是逆势反转"的争论。 搞清楚本轮行情与前四轮超级周期有一个本质区别：定价权已经从"边际消费方"转移到"库存持有方"。美国精炼铜关税预期在 18个月里把约120万吨铜吸进美国仓库，全球三大交易所库存中约七成集中在美国。这部分供给是被行政力量强制锁定的库存，不是被消费掉的库存。因此真正决定方向性的变量，不是"供需缺口有多大"，而是"这批库存什么时候、以什么价格回流"。 供给端来看：矿端2026年增速只有0.2%，进口铜精矿现货加工费跌至−231.7美元/吨的历史极值，新矿从发现到投产平均耗时16年，供给的价格弹性被压到了十年量级的"零弹性"。 需求端来看：铜杆周度开工率环比下滑21个百分点，中国未锻轧铜及铜材进口同比下降 11.5%，铝代铜在光伏等领域的推进仍在继续，价格破坏已经发生，只是还没有体现在期货价格里。 理智地看，2026年四季度到2027年上半年，铜价更可能走出"高位宽幅震荡、中枢缓慢上移"，而不是单边冲向22000美元的历史极值；但需要警惕，如果白宫一夜之间明确搁置精炼铜关税，美国库存集中的回流压力足以在半年内快速抹平全年缺口，这是潜在的不容忽视的最大下行风险。

articles.title: 不满豁免对俄制裁，担心更坏事情发生，美媒称泽连斯基决定“公开对抗特朗普”
articles.summary: 乌克兰总统泽连斯基当地时间17日称，美国政府豁免对俄罗斯实施的多项制裁措施“是错误的”，只会帮助俄罗斯人。美国《国会山报》称，这是泽连斯基对美国总统特朗普做法的“谴责”。《华尔街日报》评论称，情绪低落的泽连斯基决定“冒险公开对抗特朗普”。路透社称，从美国威胁切断对乌克兰的情报支持，到豁免俄罗斯出口关税，再到可能帮助俄罗斯为战争提供资金的柴油协议，对基辅和美乌关系而言，这是具有破坏性的一周。 泽连斯基：阻止对俄制裁“是错误的” 据乌《基辅独立报》报道，泽连斯基18日在社交媒体上表示，自从特朗普宣布“俄乌之间能源停火”以来，俄已对乌的能源、石油和天然气设施发动76次袭击。他说：“美国需要明白，俄罗斯不会因为被解除制裁或协议而作出任何让步。” 特朗普于16日签署行政令，豁免了与俄相关的关键美国制裁和关税。路透社称，豁免内容包括对该国商品征收的关税，以及对购买其石油和天然气的处罚。这些措施依据的是特朗普9月签署成为法律的《2026年格雷厄姆制裁俄罗斯和伊朗法案》。 《基辅独立报》称，泽连斯基称，特朗普进一步阻止对俄实施制裁是“错误的”。他表示，华盛顿很可能会继续放松对莫斯科的制裁，并补充说，本月初美俄达成的柴油协议“只是第一步”，未来可能还会有更多举动。此外，据路透社报道，泽连斯基16日在欧盟峰会期间谴责了特朗普与俄达成的“柴油协议”。他还称，太空探索技术公司“星链”卫星通信系统的军事化版本“星盾”的运行情况有所改善，但尚未完全恢复。一天之后，泽连斯基再次称，太空探索技术公司的卫星系统使用仍受到部分限制。据报道，泽连斯基告诉记者：“这些限制仅适用于乌克兰境内，而不适用于欧盟国家。换言之，这是一次有计划的行动。” 18日凌晨，俄第二大城市圣彼得堡遭到乌克兰武装部队的大规模无人机袭击，目标包括石油码头、数据中心和桥梁。遭袭的圣彼得堡石油码头是俄最大的燃料储存和出口设施之一。 特朗普：我的决定非常明智 美国全国广播公司称，美国国务卿鲁比奥17日说：“总统希望利用这60天的时间来分析同时实施制裁和关税对全球经济乃至美国经济意味着什么。”特朗普称，豁免制裁“是一个非常明智的决定，对国家有利，对世界也有好处”。 鲁比奥17日还回应了有关美限制乌使用“星链”系统的传言。据美国《新闻周刊》报道，鲁比奥当天告诉记者：“我不知道泽连斯基说了什么，也不确定他是否清楚自己在说什么，但这并非蓄意而为。我们与此事无关，美方没有人下令降低‘星链’的速度。”鲁比奥强调：“我知道乌想要使用‘星盾’系统。他们要求使用该系统是为了对俄境内进行纵深打击。但目前他们还没有获得使用权。” 乌《基辅邮报》18日称，这场技术争端凸显华盛顿与基辅之间在远程拦截限制以及对商业通信的依赖方面不断扩大的地缘政治摩擦。鲁比奥的否认与特朗普此前的表态相呼应。不过，知情人士透露，马斯克曾直接向特朗普提议限制卫星服务，而特朗普批准了这项措施，从而为五角大楼限制“星盾”系统的功能铺平了道路。 美国《华尔街日报》报道称，乌获取军用级“星链”终端受到限制，此举凸显了近几周来美乌关系恶化的程度。近日，特朗普提出从俄购买柴油，并呼吁泽连斯基下台。乌方怒不可遏。 俄官员：一个重要的历史性时刻 俄罗斯负责对外投资和经济合作事务的总统特别代表德米特里耶夫表示，美政府暂停实施对俄制裁法案，是一个重要的历史性时刻。据俄《消息报》17日报道，他在社交媒体平台上写道，《2026年格雷厄姆制裁俄罗斯和伊朗法案》蕴藏着使莫斯科与华盛顿之间经贸互动完全停滞的风险。德米特里耶夫解释说，维持这些限制首先会对美国企业和全球市场造成严重损害，而互利合作则符合两国的利益。 德米特里耶夫表示，俄美柴油协议仅是他与美国代表会谈可能取得的成果的开端。据美国《纽约时报》报道，知情人士透露，特朗普的特使威特科夫和女婿库什纳在与乌克兰和欧洲官员的会谈中提出，欧洲应恢复购买更多俄天然气。美方认为，为促使俄乌冲突结束，乌克兰应考虑重启曾向欧洲输送俄天然气的管道。美国政府官员认为俄罗斯天然气出口可能是和平协议的一部分。报道认为，这一提议或许是整个计划中最大胆也最具争议的部分。 本文来源： 环球时报 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 金融街论坛，预期是否兑现？
articles.summary: 摘 要 10月利率继续创新低，市场开始正式定价货币宽松的可能性。目前对金融街论坛的预期有三，包括降准降息、政策利率锚由7D切换到1D、股市支持政策。我们认为，市场期待的总量型货币宽松可能落空，降息、换锚的可能性都比较低，即使有降准，考虑到DR001中枢已经下移，对债市的实质性利好也有限；此外，央行对权益市场大概率保持支持性态度，但对股市的强力支持政策还需等待。总体看，债市利率可能先向上反弹，当然，调整的幅度和持续性都不会太强，年底前利率大概率还会有一波下行。因此交易角度可以短暂止盈，配置角度坚持调整即买入思路，久期策略占优。 历史上，金融街论坛政策增量以既有政策的细化和落地为主，且多有事前铺垫。 2023年之前，央行高层发言主要围绕既有政策及实施成效展开，新增政策信息较少。2023年以来，潘功胜行长的发言更侧重政策部署与具体工具安排，政策前瞻性和操作性有所增强。 本次金融街论坛有望释放总量宽松预期，降准的可能性大于降息。 今年以来，货币宽松主要通过结构性工具落实，叠加7月政治局会议提出“适时调整”货币政策，进一步降准降息仍有政策空间。考虑到四季度政府债供给压力，降准更有利于补充低成本长期流动性；而降息受银行净息差约束及近期结构性政策效果仍待观察等因素影响，窗口或后移至明年初。 政策利率由7天期向隔夜切换的条件尚不成熟，本次论坛直接宣布换锚的概率较低。 尽管央行逐步将短端利率调控目标转向DR001，但7天期逆回购利率仍是主要政策利率，从海外经验看，政策利率和货币市场基准期限并不必然一致。从实际操作看，隔夜逆回购尚未形成常态化操作及固定利率报价机制，跨季前后仍需依靠7天、14天期工具稳定流动性及市场预期。 资本市场支持政策或以维护市场稳定、完善既有机制为主，大规模增量支持政策的可能性相对有限。 央行近期更加关注海外资产估值回调及跨市场风险传染，而国内市场交投仍较活跃，尚未出现明显流动性压力，新设大规模股市支持工具的必要性不高。 从历史看，金融街论坛释放的政策增量对债市主要产生短期影响。 2023年结构性政策信号对债市影响有限；2024年债市短期受权益市场及资金面扰动；2025年恢复国债买卖推动利率短期下行，但利好随后消退。 报告正文 近期市场对本次金融街论坛的政策预期主要集中于三个方面：一是降准降息；二是政策利率由7天期向隔夜切换；三是出台资本市场支持政策。 结合过往金融街论坛相关政策的发布规律，我们认为，本次论坛中宣布的宽松政策可能如下：降准兑现的可能性大于降息，政策利率由7天期向隔夜切换的条件尚不成熟，资本市场支持政策则值得期待，重点或在于完善既有支持机制及推进非银流动性支持工具。 01 历年金融街论坛释放了哪些增量政策信息？ 从历年金融街论坛发言看，2023年之前，易纲行长和潘功胜副行长的发言整体以阐释既有政策、总结实施成效为主，增量信息较为有限。 2018年，易纲行长主要围绕深化金融业对内对外开放展开讲话；2019年，易纲行长聚焦深化金融供给侧结构性改革、缓解民营及小微企业融资困难，两次论坛主旨演讲均无明显增量信息。2020年，易纲行长主要围绕疫情期间的货币政策支持及下一阶段政策取向展开讲话，未释放明显增量信息；潘功胜副行长聚焦宏观审慎政策框架建设，主要增量信息为进一步明确房地产贷款集中度等宏观审慎工具的研究方向，并表示《系统重要性银行评估办法》拟于近期发布。2021年，易纲行长主要围绕发挥金融资源配置与风险管理功能、增强经济韧性展开讲话，未释放明显增量信息；潘功胜副行长聚焦美联储量化宽松退出及其外溢影响，发言中指出房地产融资风险偏好过度收缩的行为正逐步得到矫正，但未提出新的具体政策安排。2022年，易纲行长主要围绕货币政策总量与结构相结合、支持实体经济及房地产市场展开讲话，潘功胜副行长则聚焦美元周期与中国外汇市场，均未释放明显增量政策信息。 2023年潘功胜担任央行行长后，其发言进一步涉及货币政策部署及具体政策工具，政策展望和操作层面的信息有所增加。 2023年，潘功胜行长主要围绕货币政策支持实体经济、防范化解房地产及地方债务风险展开讲话，增量信息主要包括明确将为“三大工程”建设提供中长期低成本资金支持，并提出必要时央行将对债务负担较重地区提供应急流动性贷款支持。2024年，潘功胜行长主要围绕一揽子增量货币政策落实情况及中国经济高质量发展展开讲话，增量信息主要包括进一步明确年底前预计择机降准0.25—0.5个百分点、以及预计10月21日LPR下调20—25BP。2025年，潘功胜行长主要围绕宏观审慎管理体系建设及未来改革方向展开讲话，增量信息主要包括恢复公开市场国债买卖操作、研究实施一次性个人信用救济政策、研究将宏观审慎评估（MPA）拆分为货币政策执行评估和宏观审慎及金融稳定评估； 其中恢复公开市场国债买卖操作仅在25年1月暂停买入国债时提及“择机恢复”，剩余两项政策事先铺垫则更为充分。 综合来看，在讲话主题方面， 货币政策调控框架、重点领域金融支持及金融风险防范始终是金融街论坛央行高层发言的核心内容，且近年来对具体政策工具的讨论有所增加。 在政策增量方面， 2023年以来，论坛释放的政策信息更加丰富，不仅涉及既有政策的实施进展更新，也逐步出现事前铺垫相对有限的新增政策安排，政策前瞻性有所增强。 02 本次金融街论坛哪些政策预期更可能兑现？ 2.1 降准可能性大于降息 历史上，仅2024年金融街论坛曾涉及降准降息政策，但相关政策在论坛前已有充分铺垫，论坛上主要延续前期政策信号，进一步强化年内降准预期。 9月24日发布会上，潘功胜宣布近期降准0.5个百分点、下调7天期逆回购利率20BP，并表示年底前可能择机进一步降准0.25—0.5个百分点，相关降准降息政策于9月27日落地。10月18日金融街论坛上，潘功胜再次释放年底前进一步降准的信号，并预计10月21日LPR下行20—25BP。此后LPR如期下调25BP，但年内降准预期并未实现。 回顾今年货币政策调控历史可以发现，今年以来宽松政策主要通过结构性工具落实。 今年，央行年度工作会议提出灵活高效运用降准降息等工具，潘功胜随后明确表示“今年降准降息还有一定的空间”，但后续政策变更均以再贷款、PSL等结构性工具为主。年中央行虽调整政策利率走廊并且创设隔夜逆回购，但目前尚未涉及总量型宽松政策。 而9月28日的国常会出台的系列增量政策也已基本落地完，仍旧以增加再贷款额度和降低再贷款利率为主，逻辑上对前期的系列政策要有一个验证的阶段，因此我们认为后续继续追加总量型货币政策的可能性有限。 如果有总量型政策，我们认为降准的概率显著高于降息。对于降准而言， 10月9日财政部安排使用5500亿元地方政府债务结存限额，叠加年内剩余政府债发行，四季度政府债供给仍有一定压力；降准能够提供低成本的长期流动性，也有利于稳定股市，因此可能性比降息高。当然，需要注意的是，近期在没有降准的情况下，DR001的震荡区间已经提前下移，或也指向对降准不宜过度期待。 与之相对，降息则需要考虑明年的银行息差压力。 若四季度降息落地并带动LPR下调，那么约定2027年1月1日重定价的存量浮动利率贷款将于年初按照更低利率计息，对明年银行净息差形成拖累。因此，除非四季度出现明显超预期的经济金融冲击，否则从兼顾稳增长和银行息差的角度看，将降息窗口后移至明年初或更为合适。 2.2 政策利率换锚可能性较低 首先，逐步增加隔夜逆回购操作频率具备一定合理性。 随着我国货币市场交易结构变化，隔夜回购成交占比已超过90%，隔夜融资成为金融机构流动性管理的重要方式。2026年二季度货政报告明确指出，自2025年起，短端利率调控目标已由DR007逐步转向DR001，2026年以来进一步向市场明确传递了目标利率转隔夜的信号。隔夜市场利率对短期资金供求变化更为敏感，未来通过隔夜操作更精准地匹配市场需求，符合利率调控机制改革方向。 然而，货币市场基准利率变为DR001，并不必然意味着政策利率将立刻由7天期调整至隔夜。 从海外经验看，政策利率与市场利率调控目标并不需要采用相同期限。 2008年以前，欧央行通过7天期主要再融资操作（MRO）利率引导隔夜市场利率，与当前我国通过7天期逆回购利率引导DR001的调控思路异曲同工。2008年后，随着欧央行开展长期再融资操作和资产购买计划，银行体系超额准备金持续增加，隔夜市场利率逐渐围绕隔夜存款便利利率（DFR）附近运行，隔夜DFR逐步成为短期市场利率的实际锚。对我国而言，现阶段7天期逆回购利率仍能较好发挥政策利率锚的作用，立即调整主要政策利率期限的必要性相对有限。 从央行表态看， 7月15日，央行副行长邹澜明确表示，现阶段隔夜逆回购主要发挥超短期流动性调节作用，7天期逆回购操作利率仍是主要政策利率。8月公布的二季度货政报告进一步提出，将结合一级交易商需求，逐步增加隔夜逆回购操作频率。 从央行公开市场操作看，隔夜逆回购的政策利率信号机制可能尚未成熟，7天及更长期限工具仍具有不可替代的作用。 一方面，目前隔夜逆回购整体仍在特殊时点按需操作为主，尚未形成每日常态化操作，和公开固定的政策利率报价机制；另一方面，9月跨季前后，央行仍通过不同期限工具前瞻式投放，稳定资金面。9月18日和28日，央行分别开展1000亿元和3000亿元14天期逆回购，提前覆盖跨季和国庆假期前后的流动性；10月12日至16日，央行继续每日开展450亿至650亿元7天期逆回购。这表明隔夜逆回购虽已发挥短期流动性调节作用，但尚不能完全替代7天、14天期工具在稳定银行资负和金融机构预期方面的功能，隔夜操作机制的完善及市场预期引导仍需时间。 因此，我们认为本次金融街论坛直接宣布主要政策利率换锚的概率较低。 考虑到央行近期仍反复强调7天期逆回购利率的主要政策利率地位，预计本次论坛更可能侧重提高隔夜操作频率、完善短端利率调控机制，而非直接调整主要政策利率期限。 2.3 资本市场支持政策或以维护市场稳定为主 从央行表态看，资本市场支持政策或以维护市场稳定为主，大规模增量支持政策的可能性相对有限。 相较于2024年和2025年对于流动性拐点和美国关税政策的关注，央行在二季度货政报告中特别指出，“部分经济体股票市场估值偏高，流动性收紧可能触发市场回调”，并提示关注海外主要经济体货币政策调整的外溢风险；10月15日G20会议上，潘功胜进一步强调，人工智能相关资产估值回调风险加剧了全球金融脆弱性。结合今年陆家嘴论坛上潘功胜提出的“风险跨市场传染等挑战可能增多”，体现出央行对全球金融市场估值风险及跨市场风险传染的关注有所加强。 因此逻辑上讲，在估值压力消化之前，政策更可能以稳定市场为主、而非强力支持。从国内市场看，当前科技成长板块虽调整较大，但整体交投仍较活跃，尚未出现类似2024年9月的明显成交萎缩。 考虑到央行已建立证券、基金、保险公司互换便利和股票回购增持再贷款等稳市工具，预计后续政策将更侧重完善既有机制，而非再次创设大规模股市支持工具。 从央行资产负债表看，目前“对其他金融性公司债权”余额仍处于历史较低水平，尚未观察到央行对非银金融机构大规模扩张融资支持的迹象，这与央行当前侧重维护市场平稳运行、防范系统性风险的政策判断相一致。 新增政策工具方面，进一步推进特定情景下非银流动性支持机制的可能性较高。 一方面，2025年金融街论坛上，潘功胜已提出探索特定情景下向非银机构提供流动性的机制安排，今年6月陆家嘴论坛进一步明确研究设立特定情景非银流动性支持宏观审慎工具，在债券等市场出现系统性压力时向非银机构提供紧急流动性，并强调该工具并非对非银机构的常态化流动性供给。 本次论坛可能进一步披露非银流动性支持工具的研究进展，但正式出台仍存在不确定性。 03 债市怎么看？ 首先，我们认为金融街论坛后利率可能先向上反弹，原因在于前期宽松预期落空；其次，调整幅度和持续性可能相对有限，从历史来看，金融街论坛释放的政策增量只能影响债市短期定价，但其持续性仍取决于其他政策博弈，以及资金面、权益市场和机构配置行为等因素。 对于政策增量信息的市场反应，可以重点参考2023到2025年金融街论坛后的债市表现。 2023年，论坛虽释放部分结构性政策支持信号，但对债市影响相对有限。 11月8日金融街论坛上，潘功胜行长提出为“三大工程”建设提供中长期低成本资金支持，并表示必要时将对债务负担较重地区提供应急流动性支持，但未宣布全面降准降息措施。论坛后3个有效交易日，1年、5年、10年期国债收益率分别下行4.46BP、4.20BP、1.78BP，短期反应相对有限。此后，受银行负债端压力、房地产融资支持预期等因素影响，债市出现期限分化。论坛后15个交易日，1年期国债收益率累计上行10.61BP，而10年期仅上行1.94BP。 2024年金融街论坛进一步明确年内降准预期，但由于前期已有充分铺垫，债市短期反而受到权益市场走强等因素压制。 10月18日金融街论坛上，潘功胜行长再次表示年底前将视市场流动性情况择机降准0.25—0.5个百分点，预计10月21日LPR下调20—25BP，并宣布股票回购增持再贷款政策正式落地。由于降准预期此前已获释放，论坛并未带来明显超预期的货币宽松信号；同期资本市场支持政策提振权益市场情绪，叠加税期资金面收敛及增量财政政策预期扰动，债市短期承压。论坛后7个有效交易日，5年、10年期国债收益率分别上行4.86BP、5.14BP。此后，随着央行加大流动性支持、地方债供给担忧逐步消化，叠加年内进一步降准预期，债市重新走强，论坛后30个日，5年、10年期国债收益率分别下行12.07BP、8.78BP。值得注意的是，尽管年底进一步降准最终未能兑现，但市场此前已逐步将降准预期后移至2025年初，央行也通过国债买卖、买断式逆回购等工具提供流动性支持，因此债市并未出现持续性调整。 2025年，恢复公开市场国债买卖操作构成明确的政策增量，带动债市短期走强，但利好影响随后有所消退。 10月27日金融街论坛上，潘功胜行长宣布将恢复年初暂停的公开市场国债买卖操作，该政策超出市场对恢复时点的预期，带动国债收益率快速下行。论坛后3个交易日，1年、5年、10年期国债收益率分别下行8.85BP、5.65BP、3.88BP。然而，11月初公布的10月国债净买入规模仅为200亿元，低于部分机构预期，叠加前期利好逐步消化，中长期国债收益率逐渐回升。论坛后30个交易日，1年期国债收益率仍较会前下降7.02BP，而5年、10年期分别上行1.74BP、0.13BP。
